subject: Banking
title: Too Big to Fail Moral Hazard
description: A micro-lesson that makes Too Big to Fail Moral Hazard usable.

hook.text: In 2008, the government rescued big banks but let small ones fail.

buildup.text: AIG, Citigroup, and Bank of America received billions in bailouts.

discovery.text: Too-big-to-fail banks borrow at lower rates because lenders know the government will bail them out.

twist.text: Banks that received bailouts in 2008 are even bigger now.

climax.text: Bailouts create moral hazard. Each rescue encourages bigger bets because the cost of failure falls on taxpayers.

punchline.text: Bailed out in 2008. Even bigger now. The moral hazard loop continues.

quiz.question: What is the 'too big to fail' problem?
options: Large banks being rescued because their failure would crash the economy

details.summary: When banks know the government will bail them out if they fail, they take greater risks, creating moral hazard. This too-big-to-fail problem means taxpayers subsidize bank risk-taking while shareholders capture the profits.
details.whyItMatters: Moral hazard is the core paradox of modern banking. Government guarantees are necessary to prevent panics but simultaneously encourage the reckless behavior that creates the next crisis.
takeaways: Government bailout expectations reduce banks' motivation to manage risk
The 2008 bailouts confirmed to markets that large banks would be saved
Dodd-Frank attempted to end too-big-to-fail through resolution planning

faq.question: Has the too-big-to-fail problem been solved since 2008?
faq.answer: Banks now hold more capital and submit living wills describing how they could be wound down. But the largest banks are even bigger than in 2008, and the 2023 bank rescues suggest the government would still intervene during a systemic crisis.

faq.question: What is the alternative to bailing out large banks?
faq.answer: Dodd-Frank created an orderly liquidation authority to wind down failing banks without bailouts. In theory, shareholders and creditors absorb losses while essential services continue. In practice, this has never been tested on a truly systemic bank.
